doc.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001

title: Easter cantatas and 'Tongues of Fire'
summary: Brubeck discusses the Vienna cancellation, a possible London Symphony recording, and the multilingual 'Tongues of Fire' with help from a linguist friend.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Yeah. Yesterday we found out we’re not doing my Easter cantata in Vienna, which was very disappointing to Russell Gloyd, our conductor, but he said, “well then we’ll record it with the London Symphony Orchestra.” I’m trying to make up my mind whether to do the Easter cantata, which is called “Beloved Son” or “Tongues of Fire,” which is about after Christ comes back and fire descends on the disciples and they all speak in tongues and everything. That’s a very different kind of cantata. And I think it’s only been performed once, yeah. And to me it’s so wild because I had a friend of mine that lived here in Wilton that was a linguist. So I said, “each man speaking in his own tongue, are they not all Gallileans? How can they do this?” You know? And in Greek and in the language Christ used was what was used in Jerusalem. And Persian and Macedonia. So he investigated and I said, “just give me each one of those languages.” He said, “well I don’t know, some of these are ancient, Sanskrit and,” he said, “but I know professors all over the country, I’ll write to them all.” So those little things in that piece just knock me out because the choir’s got to sing in all these languages. It’s just one line that they have to sing in all the different languages. Something like “he was the son of God” or a simple line. But it’s full of the sounds of the Middle East. And also where not a lot of other composers have already done a work, it’s so hard to do an Easter cantata where the conductor and the choir can pick many great versions. So this one I’m kind of in free territory.
